target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would directly remove scheduling barriers and increase access for workers and voters
objection: A federal holiday does not force private employers to give paid time off, so many low-wage hourly workers in retail, restaurants, warehouses, cleaning, and caregiving would still have to choose between working, losing wages, or voting in unscheduled time. Therefore, the holiday would not consistently solve the scheduling barrier and could leave the most constrained low-income workers largely unchanged or even worse off.

target: AG2’s assumption that a holiday leaves low-wage workers essentially unchanged because employers are not required to give paid time off
objection: That assumption overstates how little would change in practice. AG1 argues that a federal holiday typically changes employer scheduling behavior—many businesses close, reduce hours, or staff fewer shifts—so constrained workers are often not scheduled during voting hours or can vote without the same wage-loss tradeoff. The claim that a holiday would leave them unchanged is therefore too absolute.

target: AG1’s rebuttal that holiday designation would materially change scheduling practice and free constrained workers
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably trigger the schedule restructuring AG1 assumes. In many shift-based private sectors such as retail, restaurants, cleaning, warehousing, caregiving, hospitals, and security, businesses continue operating and keep normal or staggered shifts. For those workers, the holiday still leaves them facing the same choice between missing wages and finding time to vote, so the barrier is not materially reduced.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would leave scheduling constraints essentially intact without paid leave
objection: AG1 argues that the target’s assumption is too strong because holiday designation changes operating calendars in practice: many schools and workplaces close or reduce hours, and that broader change can create workable voting windows even without a legal paid-leave mandate. The rebuttal says the holiday can materially reduce schedule conflicts despite not guaranteeing paid leave.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday observance commonly restructures schedules enough to free hourly workers
objection: AG2 says a federal holiday does not guarantee the kind of schedule restructuring AG1 describes. For many low-wage, shift-based sectors, ‘holiday’ simply means some workers still cover demand with unchanged rotations, so the holiday does not reliably reduce the work-vs-vote conflict for the most constrained workers.

target: AG2’s assumption that lack of a paid-leave mandate means the holiday is ineffective
objection: AG1 replies that the assumption ignores international precedent and practical holiday scheduling. Since 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, holiday/weekend timing is presented as a workable access lever, not merely cosmetic. AG1 says this undermines the claim that the holiday would leave the most constrained workers essentially unchanged.

target: AG1’s inference from international weekend/holiday elections to the U.S. context
objection: Other OECD countries having elections on holidays or weekends does not prove that a U.S. federal holiday would have the same effect, because labor rules, employer obligations, workplace closure norms, and voting-access institutions differ. So the international comparison does not establish that a U.S. holiday would actually give workers usable time off to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would not meaningfully change staffing or time to vote
objection: AG1 says the target relies on an overly narrow view of what a holiday does. Even without mandatory paid leave, a federal holiday changes the operating calendar, leading many schools and workplaces to close or reduce staffing and creating more feasible windows for voting. So the holiday can still materially reduce scheduling conflicts.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status itself materially reduces the workday-school-day collision
objection: AG2 counters that a federal holiday does not compel most private employers to close, reduce staffing, or provide paid voting time. Many hourly workers in retail, restaurants, warehousing, cleaning, caregiving, and other service/essential jobs can still be scheduled as usual, so the work-vs-vote collision remains.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday only changes the calendar and not access for the most constrained workers
objection: AG1 says that holiday designation does change staffing and schedule realities in practice, with many workplaces and schools following holiday calendars and reducing hours. That operational shift can create voting windows and reduce the collision even if some employers remain open.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday calendars commonly create usable scheduling flexibility for the lowest-income workers
objection: AG2 argues that the holiday does not reliably produce that flexibility because many private employers remain open and can still assign holiday shifts. Without legal time-off requirements, workers may still face the same wage-loss-or-vote tradeoff.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would not reliably materialize into time to vote for constrained workers
objection: AG1 responds that holiday designation often changes compensation and scheduling norms in practice, including holiday pay, compensatory time, and shift swaps. Those changes can soften the wage-loss problem and make voting feasible even without a legal paid-leave mandate.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is a good way to change the actual working/school calendar
objection: AG2’s main case is that the policy has a bad reliability and distributional tradeoff: it does not guarantee paid time off, does not reliably reduce the scheduling barrier for the workers most constrained by rigid shifts, and risks disadvantaging low-income workers while being less effective than reforms that directly protect voting time.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is an unreliable or harmful substitute for better reforms
objection: AG1 says that the holiday itself changes schedule realities rather than merely substituting symbolically. Because it directly targets the work/school-time collision, it reduces the practical cost of voting and has broad bipartisan and international support, so it is not as weak or harmful as the target suggests.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday designation typically creates practical coverage and scheduling flexibility for the most constrained workers
objection: AG2 says that is not guaranteed in the U.S. because a federal holiday does not require private employers to shut down, reduce staffing, or provide paid voting time. Retail, food service, warehousing, cleaning, and caregiving jobs can continue on holidays, leaving low-income workers with the same work-vs-vote tradeoff.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday leaves the work-vs-vote collision intact
objection: AG1 argues that a national holiday changes the actual calendar and staffing expectations, with schools closing and workplaces re-planning coverage. That reduces the frequency and severity of conflicts during polling hours and therefore directly lowers the voting barrier for many constrained workers.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status produces workable coverage and schedule adjustments for the most constrained workers
objection: AG2 contends that this is overbroad because the holiday does not compel employers to close, reduce staffing, or provide paid time. Many essential and service jobs stay open, so the holiday does not reliably create usable voting windows for the workers AG1 is trying to help.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is a poor substitute for reforms that directly change constraints
objection: AG1 says the holiday is not a substitute in the sense of being unrelated; it changes the same scheduling constraint by moving the day onto a holiday calendar. The policy is therefore itself a direct way of changing work/school scheduling realities.

target: AG1’s assumption that holiday status will reduce the work-vs-vote collision for the most constrained hourly workers
objection: AG2 argues that holiday scheduling often prioritizes maintaining coverage rather than freeing low-wage workers. In continuous-service jobs, employers can still staff holiday shifts with workers who have the least flexibility, so the collision remains or is shifted onto the least powerful employees.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday status mostly redistributes burden onto the least flexible workers and leaves the collision intact
objection: AG1 says that assumes too much. Holiday calendars commonly reduce operations and change coverage patterns, which directly lowers the hours when inflexible workers are scheduled during polling time. So the holiday can still reduce the collision rather than simply redistribute it.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status lowers the opportunity cost of voting for the most constrained workers
objection: AG2 says the holiday may do the opposite in many service sectors: employers keep operating on holidays and may even increase staffing for holiday demand or premium pay. Because there is no job-protected time to vote, low-income workers can still be scheduled to work, leaving the work-vs-vote tradeoff unchanged.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday incentives typically push vulnerable workers into holiday shifts
objection: AG1 responds that the assumption is contestable because holiday designation changes the whole workday calendar, not just incentives. Even where some businesses stay open, holiday scheduling and shift-swapping can create shorter, more flexible windows that make voting feasible and reduce opportunity cost.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status makes voting feasible by changing compensation and scheduling practice
objection: AG2 counters that holiday status can worsen the problem for low-wage workers if employers use the holiday to staff shifts precisely because demand is high. Since private employers still are not required to provide voting time, these workers may remain stuck working or losing income to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday status mainly changes incentives against voters
objection: AG1 says that assumes holiday status typically results in more work conflict, which is not established. The holiday changes coverage realities and staffing expectations, so the target’s claim that it usually fails for constrained workers is too strong.

target: AG1’s claim that reducing the work/school collision lowers opportunity cost enough for voting logistics
objection: AG2 says voting barriers are not only about the day being a workday. Low-income voters still face travel, childcare or eldercare coordination, procedural steps, and waiting time, and a holiday does not automatically remove those frictions or guarantee protected time to handle them.

target: AG2’s claim that a freed day will not meaningfully lower voting opportunity cost because logistics remain
objection: AG1 answers that the work/school-time collision is the binding constraint for many voters, and freeing that day gives them the time needed to handle travel, childcare, and procedural steps. So even if it does not solve every friction, the holiday still lowers opportunity cost by relaxing the main time constraint.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday-created extra time will be usable for voting logistics
objection: AG2 says that assumes the most constrained workers are actually free on the holiday, which is often false. Because private employers are not required to restructure coverage or provide job-protected voting time, many low-wage workers remain scheduled and therefore do not get the extra time the holiday is supposed to create.
